name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTGROWTHANDDEVELOPMENT_MATCH_Q01 - Chemical nature of plant growth regulators

questiontext.text:
Match the plant growth regulators with their respective chemical classes and choose the correct combination.

List I (Plant Growth Regulator)List II (Chemical Nature)
(A) Indole-3-acetic acid (IAA)(i) Terpene
(B) Kinetin(ii) Carotenoid derivative
(C) Abscisic acid (ABA)(iii) Indole compound
(D) Gibberellic acid (\(\text{GA}_3\))(iv) Adenine derivative

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Plant growth regulators (PGRs) are small, simple molecules belonging to diverse chemical groups: indole compounds, adenine derivatives, carotenoid derivatives, terpenes, and gases.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pair
1. Indole-3-acetic acid (IAA) is an auxin chemically classified as an indole compound.
2. Kinetin (\(N^6\)-furfurylamino purine) is a cytokinin chemically classified as an adenine (purine) derivative.
3. Abscisic acid (ABA) is a growth-inhibiting hormone derived from carotenoids.
4. Gibberellic acid (\(\text{GA}_3\)) is a gibberellin chemically classified as a terpene.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct biological pairings are: Indole-3-acetic acid with indole compound, Kinetin with adenine derivative, Abscisic acid with carotenoid derivative, and Gibberellic acid with terpene.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTGROWTHANDDEVELOPMENT_MATCH_Q02 - Scientists and discovery of plant hormones

questiontext.text:
Match the scientists with their key discoveries related to plant growth regulators and select the correct combination.

List I (Scientist)List II (Contribution)
(A) Charles Darwin and Francis Darwin(i) Isolated auxin from oat coleoptile tips
(B) F.W. Went(ii) Confirmed release of volatile ethylene from ripened oranges
(C) E. Kurosawa(iii) Observed phototropism in canary grass coleoptiles
(D) H.H. Cousins(iv) Induced 'bakanae' symptoms using sterile fungal filtrates

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Each of the five major groups of plant growth regulators was discovered through classical physiological observations and experiments.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pair
1. Charles Darwin and his son Francis Darwin observed that coleoptiles of canary grass responded to unilateral illumination by growing toward the light source (phototropism).
2. F.W. Went isolated auxin from the tips of coleoptiles of oat seedlings.
3. E. Kurosawa (1926) reported the appearance of 'bakanae' (foolish seedling) disease symptoms in rice seedlings treated with sterile filtrates of the fungus Gibberella fujikuroi.
4. H.H. Cousins (1910) confirmed the release of a volatile substance (later identified as ethylene) from ripened oranges that hastened the ripening of stored unripened bananas.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The accurate pairings are: Charles Darwin and Francis Darwin with phototropism in canary grass coleoptiles, F.W. Went with isolation of auxin from oat coleoptile tips, E. Kurosawa with 'bakanae' symptoms from sterile fungal filtrates, and H.H. Cousins with volatile ethylene from ripened oranges.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTGROWTHANDDEVELOPMENT_MATCH_Q03 - Parameters used to measure plant growth

questiontext.text:
Match the plant systems with the primary parameter used to express their growth and select the correct combination.

List I (Plant System)List II (Growth Parameter)
(A) Maize root apical meristem(i) Increase in cell number
(B) Watermelon cells(ii) Increase in cell size
(C) Pollen tube(iii) Increase in length
(D) Dorsiventral leaf(iv) Increase in surface area

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Because an increase in protoplasm is difficult to measure directly, plant growth is measured using proportional parameters such as cell number, cell size, length, surface area, volume, fresh weight, and dry weight.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pair
1. A single maize root apical meristem can give rise to more than 17,500 new cells per hour, expressing growth as an increase in cell number.
2. Cells in a watermelon may increase in size by up to 3,50,000 times, expressing growth as an increase in cell size.
3. Growth of a pollen tube is measured in terms of its linear extension (length).
4. Growth in a dorsiventral leaf is denoted by an increase in its surface area.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are: Maize root apical meristem with increase in cell number, Watermelon cells with increase in cell size, Pollen tube with increase in length, and Dorsiventral leaf with increase in surface area.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTGROWTHANDDEVELOPMENT_MATCH_Q04 - Phases of growth and cellular differentiation

questiontext.text:
Match the growth phases and differentiation events with their characteristic cellular features and select the correct combination.

List I (Phase / Process)List II (Cellular Characteristics)
(A) Meristematic phase(i) Increased vacuolation, cell enlargement, new cell wall deposition
(B) Phase of elongation(ii) Rich in protoplasm, large nuclei, thin cellulosic walls
(C) Phase of maturation(iii) Loss of protoplasm and strong lignocellulosic secondary wall
(D) Tracheary element differentiation(iv) Maximal size with wall thickening and protoplasmic modifications

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Plant growth at root and shoot apices progresses through three distinct phases—meristematic, elongation, and maturation—followed by specific structural differentiation for specialised functions.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pair
1. Cells in the meristematic phase are rich in protoplasm, possess large conspicuous nuclei, and have thin, primary cellulosic walls with abundant plasmodesmatal connections.
2. Cells in the phase of elongation (proximal to the meristematic zone) show increased vacuolation, cell enlargement, and new cell wall deposition.
3. Cells in the phase of maturation attain their maximal size in terms of wall thickening and protoplasmic modifications.
4. During differentiation into a tracheary element, cells lose their protoplasm and develop strong, elastic, lignocellulosic secondary cell walls to conduct water under extreme tension.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, Meristematic phase pairs with rich protoplasm and thin cellulosic walls, Phase of elongation pairs with increased vacuolation and new cell wall deposition, Phase of maturation pairs with maximal size and wall thickening, and Tracheary element differentiation pairs with loss of protoplasm and lignocellulosic secondary wall.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTGROWTHANDDEVELOPMENT_MATCH_Q05 - Agricultural applications of auxins and gibberellins

questiontext.text:
Match the agricultural or horticultural applications with the corresponding plant growth regulator and select the correct combination.

List I (Application)List II (PGR / Compound)
(A) Selective killing of dicotyledonous weeds in lawns(i) Gibberellins
(B) Bolting in rosette plants such as beet and cabbage(ii) 2, 4-D
(C) Speeding up malting process in brewing industry(iii) Natural auxins (IAA / IBA)
(D) Initiating rooting in stem cuttings(iv) \(\text{GA}_3\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Auxins and gibberellins are growth-promoting PGRs widely used in agriculture, horticulture, and industry for targeted physiological responses.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pair
1. 2, 4-D is a synthetic auxin widely used as a herbicide to kill dicotyledonous weeds without affecting mature monocotyledonous lawn grasses.
2. Gibberellins promote bolting (internode elongation just prior to flowering) in beet, cabbages, and many plants with a rosette habit.
3. \(\text{GA}_3\) is specifically used to speed up the malting process in the brewing industry.
4. Auxins such as IAA and IBA help initiate rooting in stem cuttings for plant propagation.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are: selective weed control with 2, 4-D, bolting in rosette plants with gibberellins, malting acceleration with \(\text{GA}_3\), and rooting in stem cuttings with auxins.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTGROWTHANDDEVELOPMENT_MATCH_Q06 - Physiological effects of ethylene and ethephon

questiontext.text:
Match the plant responses induced by ethylene or ethephon with the correct physiological descriptions.

List I (Plant / Process)List II (Ethylene Effect)
(A) Respiratory climactic(i) Rise in respiration rate during fruit ripening
(B) Deep water rice plants(ii) Rapid internode or petiole elongation
(C) Cucumber(iii) Promotion of female flowers to increase yield
(D) Dicot seedlings(iv) Horizontal growth, axis swelling, apical hook formation

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Ethylene is a gaseous PGR, and ethephon is its widely used aqueous source in agriculture, regulating ripening, senescence, abscission, and specialised growth adaptations.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pair
1. During fruit ripening, ethylene enhances the rate of respiration; this rise is termed respiratory climactic.
2. In deep water rice plants, ethylene promotes rapid internode or petiole elongation so leaves and upper shoot parts remain above water.
3. Ethephon promotes female flowers in cucumbers, thereby increasing crop yield.
4. In dicot seedlings, ethylene induces horizontal growth of seedlings, swelling of the axis, and apical hook formation.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Each process corresponds directly to its respective physiological effect: respiratory climactic with increased respiration during ripening, deep water rice with rapid internode elongation, cucumber with female flower promotion, and dicot seedlings with horizontal growth, axis swelling, and apical hook formation.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTGROWTHANDDEVELOPMENT_MATCH_Q07 - Selecting appropriate PGRs for physiological effects

questiontext.text:
Match each desired physiological outcome in a plant with the most appropriate plant growth regulator (PGR) and select the correct combination.

List I (Desired Outcome)List II (Most Suitable PGR)
(A) Delay leaf senescence via nutrient mobilisation(i) Ethylene
(B) Induce immediate stomatal closure during stress(ii) Gibberellin
(C) Hasten maturity and early seed production in juvenile conifers(iii) Abscisic acid
(D) Synchronise fruit-set in pineapples and induce flowering in mango(iv) Cytokinin

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Each major group of plant growth regulators has distinct physiological roles in controlling senescence, stress responses, juvenility, and flowering/fruit-set.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pair
1. Cytokinins promote nutrient mobilisation, which helps delay leaf senescence.
2. Abscisic acid (ABA), known as the stress hormone, stimulates the closure of stomata and increases plant tolerance to stresses.
3. Spraying juvenile conifers with gibberellins hastens the maturity period, leading to early seed production.
4. Ethylene is used to initiate flowering and synchronise fruit-set in pineapples, and it also induces flowering in mango.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are: delaying leaf senescence with cytokinin, immediate stomatal closure with abscisic acid, hastening maturity in juvenile conifers with gibberellin, and synchronising pineapple fruit-set with ethylene.

questiontext.text:
Match the developmental phenomena with their appropriate plant examples and select the correct combination.

List I (Developmental Phenomenon)List II (Plant Example)
(A) Heterophylly due to environment(i) Cotton, coriander, and larkspur
(B) Heterophylly due to phases of life(ii) Sugarbeet, cabbages, and carrots
(C) Monocarpic biennials stimulated by cold treatment(iii) Buttercup
(D) Flowering with no correlation to light duration(iv) Day-neutral plants

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Plant development exhibits plasticity (varying structural pathways in response to environment or life phase) as well as flowering regulation by light duration (photoperiodism) and low temperature (vernalisation).

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pair
1. In buttercup, the difference in shapes of leaves produced in air versus water represents heterophyllous development due to the environment.
2. In cotton, coriander, and larkspur, juvenile leaves differ in shape from mature leaves, representing heterophylly due to phases of life.
3. Sugarbeet, cabbages, and carrots are common monocarpic biennials in which cold treatment stimulates a subsequent photoperiodic flowering response.
4. Plants in which there is no correlation between exposure to light duration and induction of flowering are termed day-neutral plants.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The accurate pairings are: environmental heterophylly with buttercup, life-phase heterophylly with cotton, coriander, and larkspur, cold-stimulated biennials with sugarbeet, cabbages, and carrots, and light-independent flowering with day-neutral plants.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PLANTGROWTHANDDEVELOPMENT_MATCH_Q09 - Causes and methods of overcoming seed dormancy

questiontext.text:
Match the aspects of seed dormancy with their respective agents or mechanisms and select the correct combination.

List I (Dormancy Aspect)List II (Agent / Mechanism)
(A) Chemical inhibitors causing endogenous dormancy(i) Microbial action and animal digestive tract
(B) Natural abrasion of impermeable seed coat(ii) Para-ascorbic acid and phenolic acids
(C) Man-made mechanical scarification(iii) Gibberellic acid and nitrates
(D) Chemicals used to overcome inhibitory substances(iv) Knives, sandpaper, or vigorous shaking

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Seed dormancy is an endogenous state where seeds fail to germinate even under favourable external conditions due to hard seed coats, immature embryos, or chemical inhibitors, and it can be broken naturally or artificially.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pair
1. Chemical inhibitors causing seed dormancy include abscisic acid, phenolic acids, and para-ascorbic acid.
2. In nature, abrasions that break the impermeable hard seed coat barrier are caused by microbial action and passage through the digestive tract of animals.
3. Man-made mechanical abrasions to break the seed coat barrier use knives, sandpaper, or vigorous shaking.
4. The effect of inhibitory substances can be removed by subjecting seeds to chilling conditions or applying chemicals such as gibberellic acid and nitrates.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are: chemical inhibitors with para-ascorbic acid and phenolic acids, natural seed coat abrasion with microbial action and animal digestive tract, man-made mechanical scarification with knives, sandpaper, or vigorous shaking, and chemical overcoming of inhibitors with gibberellic acid and nitrates.
